A data story

The risk didn't grow.
It changed hands.

Every country depends on suppliers it could lose overnight. This is the foundation of a scrollytelling piece built on that idea, real BACI trade data throughout: what the Import and Export Risk Index actually measure, and the one chart every finding in this project traces back to. The rest of the story, Türkiye's own thirty-year rotation, is being rebuilt scene by scene from here.

scroll ↓

 

 
Scene 1 / 18

What even is this number?

The usual question is "how much do you import from a country?" The better question is "could you replace that supplier tomorrow?" Two countries can buy the exact same share of their steel from abroad, one from five suppliers, one from a single supplier, and face wildly different risk. It isn't hypothetical: 34.7% of Türkiye's own import value already comes from products where a single supplier holds half the market or more. The Import Risk Index scores that difference. Try it, using the buttons and slider above the chart.

The formula multiplies each sector's share of a country's imports by how concentrated its suppliers are (a Herfindahl index, where 1.0 means a single supplier), then discounts that by how easily buyers can substitute between supplier countries for that good, an elasticity estimated per sector by Broda, Greenfield and Weinstein. Because the math is additive, a claim like "China is 33% of Türkiye's import risk" isn't an estimate, it's an exact accounting identity that sums to the total. Figures throughout use the "core" basis, excluding gold, which is volatile and swamps the Import Risk Index in years of heavy bullion flows.

Scene 2 / 18

Two numbers to keep in mind

Türkiye has two of these scores, not one: an Import Risk Index for what it buys, and an Export Risk Index for what it sells. Both measure the same idea, concentration discounted by how easy substitution is, just pointed in opposite directions. Over thirty years they've told completely different stories: imports held a flat, unremarkable band while exports fell by more than half. The rest of this story is about why.

The Import Risk Index sums each sector's import share times its supplier concentration (HHI) times a switching-difficulty discount, 1/(1+σ). The Export Risk Index drops that last term, the underlying elasticity data is only estimated for imports, so it's just export share times destination concentration. Both are sums over the same list of sectors, which is what makes the two lines directly comparable in shape, even though the switching-difficulty term means they're not on identical footing.

Scene 3 / 18

Same number, new owner

Türkiye's Import Risk Index sat in a flat 22 to 28 band for 25 years, then climbed five years straight to 27.4 by 2024, its highest since 2002. Underneath that flat line, the composition reversed completely: China rose from 1.8% of the risk to 34.6%, passing the USA in 2004, Germany in 2006, and the entire EU-27 in 2013, while the EU and US together fell from 62% to 24%. China and Russia now carry 54% between them.

This is the two-panel view every finding in this project traces back to. The next several scenes unpack each half on its own: Türkiye's own line in more detail, then the rotation with a year slider so you can trace any single partner's path.

Scene 4 / 18

Size is not risk

If risk simply tracked how much Türkiye buys from a country, these two dots would sit on top of each other. In 2024, China supplies 15% of imports but 34.6% of the risk, a 2.26× multiplier; Russia's is almost identical, 2.15×. Brazil's is the widest of all, 3.07×, on a tiny import base. Germany, the single biggest supplier here, sits at 0.90×, almost exactly proportional, the benchmark for benign size. Drag the slider below the chart to see how these gaps have moved since 1995.

The multiplier is this index's own formula rolled up per partner: HHI times the switching-difficulty discount, summed over whichever sectors that country supplies. China and Russia dominate precisely the hardest-to-substitute sectors, not just the biggest ones, which is why their risk share consistently outruns their import share. Brazil's multiplier is the highest of the twelve despite a small import share, concentrated in a handful of agricultural commodities (soy, coffee, beef) with few substitute suppliers. Germany and France sit close to 1×: broad, diversified baskets where size and risk roughly track each other.

Scene 5 / 18

Why the small numbers lie

Drag the slider below the chart to trace twelve of Türkiye's major partners' paths since 1995, colored by region. China's dot has walked steadily up and to the right: 2% of Türkiye's imports and barely more risk in 1995; by 2024 it's 15% of imports but 35% of the risk, 2.3× its weight. Germany's dot has drifted the other way, from 1.5× its import share in 1995 to 0.9× by then, a similar-sized supplier that has grown steadily more replaceable. Size and risk are not the same thing, and which countries carry the gap between them keeps changing.

China and Russia each contribute roughly twice their import weight to Türkiye's risk total; Brazil contributes about three times its weight. Japan sits at the opposite extreme: 1.5% of imports, but only 0.3% of the risk, because Japanese goods are easy to source elsewhere. The Russia and China cases aren't the same kind of dependence, though. Russia dominates products where the world market is genuinely deep (it's just 5% of world oil-product exports, 11% of wheat), so switching is expensive but possible. Where China dominates, it's often also the world's largest exporter for that product, 59% of the value in the sectors it leads, so there's frequently nowhere else at scale to buy from.

Toggle to exports for Türkiye's top buyers instead of suppliers: Germany still leads but at a shrinking multiplier, and Iraq's dot doesn't exist before 2003.

Scene 6 / 18

Most of Türkiye's concentration is a choice

Compare Türkiye's supplier concentration in each sector to the same sector in nine peer economies. Where Türkiye sits above its peers but the sector itself is diversified worldwide, that's a procurement choice, not a market fact, 22% of import value falls in that fixable zone, led by a single sector: refined fuels, $27.6bn. Only 8% is concentrated for everyone, aircraft, displays, wheat, a function of how the global market is built. Drag the slider below the chart to see how the two zones have shifted since 1995.

There's a related asymmetry worth noting: Türkiye's single biggest import line, machinery and vehicles at 40% of the import bill, is actually one of its least risky, contributing only 27% of total risk, because nearly every country sells them. Across the board, medium-tech goods carry less risk than their size would suggest (an amplification of 0.67, meaning risk share runs well below import share), while every other tier, high-tech, resource-based, low-tech and primary goods, runs at or above its import weight. The pattern holds across dozens of major economies, not just Türkiye.

Scene 7 / 18

The long rotation

Six of Türkiye's biggest import-risk sectors, thirty years each. In 1995 the single largest risk was American aircraft, Boeing alone held 60% of that market. Energy risk never actually left the top of the list, it just changed owners: Russia, then the Algeria gas era, then Russia again, now at 42% and a record 4.3 contribution. The electronics complex tells the same story in miniature, German equipment, then Sweden's Ericsson-era phones, then China from 2003, now 60%. Iron and steel has been ex-Soviet the whole way through, Ukraine first, Russia ever since. Cars are the exception: Germany, diversified and benign, for all thirty years. Hover any line for the year-by-year detail.

These six sectors aren't an arbitrary sample, they're chosen because each one has spent real time at or near the top of Türkiye's import-risk ranking at some point since 1995. Reading them side by side is what motivates the rest of this project's partner-rotation story: the aggregate risk index barely moved for two and a half decades, but that flatness hid a sector-by-sector reshuffling of exactly who Türkiye would struggle to replace, and in which product.

Scene 8 / 18

The technology ladder

Split the same thirty years by what kind of good, not which sector or partner. On the export side the change is total: the low-tech apparel cluster that once carried 55% of export risk is down to 23%, medium technology, vehicles and machinery, rose from 14% to 34%, and the export index itself fell 58% in the process. Türkiye climbed the technology ladder and de-risked by doing it. The import side tells the opposite story: after thirty years the mix sits almost exactly where it started, high tech 18% to 20%, medium tech 32% to 27%. What changed on the import side in thirty years was never what Türkiye depends on, only who it depends on for it. Hover either panel for any year's exact split.

The classification is Lall (2000), taken from UNCTADstat's own published SITC Rev.3 implementation rather than re-keyed from the paper, bridged to BACI through the HS6-to- SITC3 conversion tables. Because the index is a sum over sectors, the tier split is exact: every point of risk lands in exactly one of five tiers (primary, resource-based, low, medium, or high technology), with a residual under 2% held in totals but excluded from the tier percentages here. This chart is also the reason "size is not risk" and "the long rotation" earlier in this story don't contradict each other, the aggregate index and the partner mix can rotate completely while the underlying technology composition of what's actually being imported barely moves.

Scene 9 / 18

Money buys machines

The technology version of "size is not risk," for every major economy at once. Each dot is one tier of one country's import bill: how much of its spending goes there against how much of its import risk it carries. Medium technology, machinery and vehicles, the single biggest line in almost every country's import bill, sits consistently below the diagonal: expensive, but sold by dozens of countries, so it buys little fragility. Everything else sits above it. For Türkiye specifically, high technology is the sharpest amplifier at 1.49×, 20% of the risk on just 13% of the spending, then resource-based goods at 1.24× and low tech at 1.14×, while medium tech runs at 0.67×, 41% of the import bill carrying only 27% of the risk.

The pattern holds well beyond Türkiye: across the 59 major economies in this chart, the median amplification for medium tech is 0.70× and every other tier runs at or above 1.0×. The extremes sit at either end of the same logic: Slovenia's high-tech amplifier reaches 2.34× and India's 1.70×, while Hong Kong draws 75% of its entire import risk from high tech alone, a small, concentrated basket of chips and electronics components with few substitute suppliers, the opposite of medium tech's large, diversified, low-risk-per-dollar profile.

Scene 10 / 18

Tiny money, absolute chokepoints

Eight raw materials that barely register next to everything above: together they're about 0.3% of Türkiye's entire import bill. But each one is sourced almost entirely from one country. Russia supplies 100% of vanadium oxides ($20m in 2024); China supplies 95% of magnesium ($24m), 85% of NdFeB magnets ($35m, the material inside most electric motors and wind turbines), 70% of bauxite ($24m) and 60% of silicon metal ($28m); Morocco supplies 88% of phosphate rock ($72m, the input to fertiliser); South Africa supplies 71% of manganese ore ($28m). A value-weighted risk index, built to track hundreds of billions of dollars of trade, cannot see $20-70m chokepoints like these, they have to be flagged separately. Click any bar for that material's full import history by year and supplier.

Source: BACI, Türkiye as importer, HS6 detail for each material's exact tariff line, 1995-2024 (2024 itself pulled from the current HS classification directly, since the backward-converted 30-year series doesn't preserve every product code 1-for-1 across classification revisions, earlier years use that 30-year series, the only one that spans this far back). Unlike every other chart in this story, this one is not value-weighted or aggregated into the risk index at all, it's a deliberately separate lens for exactly the kind of position a $2-trillion-a-year index would average away. None of these eight materials is a rounding error waiting to happen: every one of them has moved real money in most years since 1995, some in wild swings (phosphate rock alone ranged from $1.3m to $123m year to year), just never enough to matter to an aggregate that only cares about hundreds of billions.

Scene 11 / 18

The chokepoints you've never heard of

These are the products, not the countries, where a broken relationship would actually hurt: Türkiye imports of a single item, worth real money, from one dominant supplier. Drag the slider below the chart to see the top 10 by value for any year back to 1995, sorted here by how concentrated each one is, highest supplier share at top. Fossil fuels almost always take several of the top slots, but which country supplies them keeps changing, Russia, Algeria and Azerbaijan have each held the top natural-gas slot at different points. Aircraft, cars, steel and electronics fill out the rest, one dominant seller at a time, rarely the same one for long. In 2024, the single largest chokepoint by value is refined petroleum products: Russian Federation holds 57% of that import, worth $20.0bn.

Concentration measured at the broad sector level badly understates the real picture: the value-weighted supplier HHI is 0.14 at that resolution but 0.29 once you look at the finer, product level, and 34.7% of Türkiye's import value comes from products where a single supplier already holds half the market or more. The most extreme cases are cheap by value but near-total by supplier share, the same handful of materials the previous scene drills into one at a time.

Scene 12 / 18

What Ankara holds

The mirror of every chokepoint scene above: 14 products (over $200m world markets each) where Türkiye itself is the dominant world exporter, sorted by how concentrated Türkiye's own grip is, highest world-export share at top. Drag the slider to see any year back to 1995. Boron products (refined borax, natural borates) are the one critical-raw-material chokepoint Türkiye owns, and its main buyer is China, the mirror image of Türkiye's own magnesium dependence. In 2024, the tightest grip is synthetic filament yarn: Türkiye holds 86% of the world market, its top buyer is United Kingdom, worth $243.5m.

The buyer labels matter as much as the share itself: leverage runs both ways when one customer takes most of what Türkiye sells, China buys 48% of Türkiye's refined borax and 63% of its cut marble, Russia buys 73% of its frozen trout, the USA buys 72% of its hunting shotguns. One product, drones (UAVs), shows a real 2024 figure but nothing at all in earlier years, that's a genuine classification gap, not a sudden emergence: UAVs never had their own tariff line before the current product classification, so pre-2024 trade in them is unrecoverable, buried inside general aircraft categories with no way to isolate it. Four other products (synthetic filament yarn, frozen trout, natural borates, fresh seabass) look similar at first, a small or middling 2023 share jumping sharply in 2024, but that jump is a change in exactly what's being measured, not a one-year swing: these four are shown pre-2024 as a broader product basket (their older tariff line covers more variants than today's narrower one), so the pre-2024 share is real trade, just for a wider category than 2024's figure. The remaining nine products' full histories are both real and measuring the same product throughout, several (machine-woven carpets, cut marble, hunting shotguns) show genuine decades-long growth from single-digit to majority world shares.

Scene 13 / 18

Where Türkiye is the dominant world seller

The same idea as the previous scene, recomputed fresh every year rather than fixed to 14 hand-picked products: whichever ten products give Türkiye its highest share of world exports that year, re-ranked as the slider moves. The same handful of Anatolian commodities keep reappearing, dried apricots, hazelnuts, refined borax, machine-woven carpets, though the buyer often changes (China only became the biggest buyer of Turkish marble after 2010). In 2024, the top example is synthetic filament yarn: Türkiye holds 86% of the world market, and United Kingdom alone buys 39% of it, worth $243.5m.

Across 36 products with world markets worth over $200m each, Türkiye supplies at least a fifth of global exports, and for several it's the outright dominant seller: refined borax (64% of world exports), dried apricots (74%), hazelnuts (62%), machine-woven carpets (66%) and, more recently, drones (around 65%). These are the mirror image of the chokepoints two scenes back, sectors where Türkiye, not some foreign supplier, is the one other countries would struggle to replace.

Scene 14 / 18

The great retracement

Zooming out from Türkiye to the world: the median import-concentration index across all 87 economies in the sample fell from 49 in 1995 to 45 by 2008, the high tide of hyper-globalization, as countries broadly diversified their supplier base. It has since climbed straight back to 49 in 2024, exactly where it started. Everything the globalization era achieved in spreading out the median country's imports has been given back in the fifteen years since.

This is the macro backdrop behind every Türkiye-specific chart above: fragmentation isn't just a story about a handful of superpowers weaponizing trade, it shows up directly in the typical country's own import structure. The shaded band is the interquartile range across the 87-country panel each year, not error bars: it shows how spread out countries are around the median, and that spread hasn't narrowed even as the median itself round-tripped back to its 1995 level.

Scene 15 / 18

Russia is now the most import-concentrated major economy

Ranking 29 major economies by the same import-concentration index, every year back to 1995. Red always marks whichever economy is most concentrated that year, not a fixed highlight on Russia, and the number inside each bar is its change from the year before. Drag the slider and watch Russia's bar: flat in the 30s and 40s for nearly three decades, rarely the reddest bar on the chart, then a straight vertical climb after 2022 as sanctions cut off its usual Western suppliers and compressed its import basket into near-total dependence on China. In 2024, Russia tops the list at 91, the highest of any major economy shown. Türkiye (gold) sits at rank 25 of 29, at 27, one of the most diversified importers here.

Source: the same 87-country, 30-year panel behind the previous scene's world-median chart (`panel_hs92_1995_2024.csv`), narrowed to 29 recognizable major economies rather than all 87. Belgium's pre-1999 rows are booked under BACI's old combined "Belgium-Luxembourg" code and were merged into one continuous Belgium series; South Africa has no rows at all before 2000 in this panel and is simply left off the ranking in those years rather than shown at a false zero, so its bar has no year-over-year figure in 2000 either, there is no 1999 value to compare against. The chart-pack's own version of this chart is a 2024-only snapshot with no year-over-year figure at all; both the slider and the per-bar change figure are new, added to show the sanctions shock as a trajectory rather than a single frozen year.

Scene 16 / 18

One economy, two orbits

Every major economy positioned by how much of its import risk points at China (horizontal) versus the United States (vertical), every year back to 1995. The world splits into an L-shape: a broad China orbit stretched along the bottom, a compact US orbit up the left column, and a diversified European cluster near the origin. Faint dust behind each dot marks its own position at five-year intervals back to 1995, no connecting line, so a dot can visibly change color if that economy's own top risk partner shifted over the decades. Drag the slider and watch entire regions migrate between orbits. In 2024, China is the top risk partner for 37 of 65 major economies shown, the United States for 6, and an EU economy for 13. Türkiye (ringed) sits at China 33% / USA 4%.

Source: `partner_exposure_2024.csv` (current HS22 classification) for 2024, and a new 1995-2023 extraction streamed from `BACI_HS92_V202601.zip` for the historical trail, the same two-vintage reconciliation already used for scenes 10 and 12, since HS92 is the only classification spanning all 30 years. The 65-country roster is fixed at 2024's "imports over $18bn" cutoff, matching the chart-pack's own selection, and tracked across all 30 years, so a country's dust trail is always comparable to its own later position; it is not re-selected year to year. One small note: the chart-pack's own printed caption for this chart ("China 37, USA 8, Germany 10") was computed at a looser $15bn cutoff than the chart it actually plots ($18bn); this rebuild's live figures always match what's on screen (37 / 6 / 13, with 9 more "other").

Scene 17 / 18

Whose factory? China's grip on the world's import risk

For each major economy, China's raw share of imports (pale dot) versus China's share of the import-risk index (solid dot), every year back to 1995. The gap between the two is the amplification, China dominates the concentrated, hard-to-switch sectors, so its risk share consistently runs well above its trade share. In 2024, Russia tops the list at 86% risk share against 57% import share. Türkiye (gold) sits at 15% imports / 33% risk, a 2.2× amplification, shown for reference alongside Germany and the USA regardless of where they rank.

Chart-pack Story 16/18. Same 65-country roster and two-vintage split as the previous scene (2024 from the current HS22 classification, 1995-2023 streamed from `BACI_HS92_V202601.zip`); the source script's own cutoff for this chart is a looser "imports over $15bn" than the $18bn roster reused here, close enough not to warrant a third near-identical extraction. Rows are the top 15 countries by that year's China risk share, re-picked every year the slider moves, so the list itself can reshuffle; Türkiye, Germany and the USA are always shown even when they fall outside the top 15, matching the source chart's own reference-economy treatment.

Scene 18 / 18

Import Risk Index: countries vs. the EU as one supplier

Treat the EU-27 as a single supplier, one customs union, one sanctions policy, and every country's measured Import Risk Index changes, some far more than others. Pale dot = the index with EU members counted separately, solid dot = EU-27 as one bloc. In 2024, Türkiye's index moves 27 → 51 (+24), ranking 9 of 10 reference economies shown, less EU-locked than every one of its neighbors tested here: Switzerland, Norway, North Macedonia, the UK, Morocco and Tunisia all move further. Drag the slider back to 1995 and watch Türkiye's own EU-bloc premium shrink from roughly +35 to today's +24, the same thirty-year diversification story the rest of this page tells, seen through one more lens.

StoryLine's own final scene, ported here with a year slider the original (2024-only) lacked. Recomputes each country's whole import-risk index with every EU-27 exporter merged into one pseudo-supplier before the sigma/HHI formula runs (`eu_as_bloc.py`'s own methodology, unchanged), compared against the standard index with EU members counted separately. Ten fixed reference countries, the exact set StoryLine's version used: Türkiye plus its neighbors (Switzerland, Norway, North Macedonia, UK, Morocco, Tunisia) and three global references (Japan, USA, China) -- not re-selected year to year, since the point is each of these ten economies' own trajectory, not a ranking that reshuffles its cast. 2024's numbers come verbatim from the original HS22 run behind StoryLine's published chart; 1995- 2023 pairs the standard index already on hand (`panel_hs92_1995_2024.csv`) with a fresh HS92-streamed extraction of the EU-bloc version, same two-vintage split used throughout this rebuild rather than mixing classifications within one year.

The throughline

The risk didn't grow. It changed hands.

Thirty years of BACI trade data all point the same direction: Türkiye's Import Risk Index sat in a flat 22-28 band the whole time, while the countries behind it changed completely, China from a rounding error to over a third of the risk, passing the EU, then the USA. That single migration explains most of what the chapters above found: why size and risk aren't the same thing, why a handful of $20-70m chokepoints matter more than their value suggests, and why what Türkiye itself holds runs through boron and drones rather than its biggest export lines. Türkiye's own rotation took thirty years, one supplier share-point at a time, driven by ordinary market shifts rather than any single event. Russia shows the same index arithmetic without that slack: unremarkable for decades, then to the world's highest in two years once sanctions cut off the alternatives it used to have, a reminder that concentration is a choice until the day it no longer is.

Data: UN Comtrade / CEPII BACI trade flows, 1995-2024. Import Risk Index = supplier concentration (HHI) discounted by ease of substitution, summed by import share; 2024 patched from the current HS classification where it and the 30-year HS92 series diverge. Sabancı University IPM, Türkiye geopolitical trade-dependence project.
